title: State Supreme Court removed Anne Arundel Orphans’ Court judge for ‘egregious misconduct’
summary: The Supreme Court of Maryland said it removed Anne Arundel Orphan's Court Judge Marc Knapp from the bench last month because of conduct that was "fundamentally incompatible with judicial office."
content:
by Will Hammann, Maryland Matters July 20, 2026

by Will Hammann, Maryland Matters July 20, 2026

The Supreme Court of Maryland said it removed Anne Arundel Orphan’s Court Judge Marc Knapp from the bench last month because of conduct that was “fundamentally incompatible with judicial office.”

The court’s unanimous 75-page opinion, released Friday, explains the reasoning behind its June 4 removal of Knapp after an investigation that was sparked by a dramatic series of run-ins with Orphans’ Court Chief Judge Vickie Gipson.

That investigation uncovered Knapp’s publicly disrespectful behavior, failure to cooperate with colleagues and even behavior “reasonably perceived as prejudiced or biased,” Justice Brynja Booth wrote for the court. But the “headliner in Judge Knapp’s lineup of misconduct” came when he deleted recordings he made of fellow judges without their consent, in front of police officers who were questioning him on the issue.

“It is antithetical to the rule of law that a judge would attempt to destroy evidence that purportedly evinced his own violations of law,” Booth wrote. “Such conduct is – without a doubt – fundamentally incompatible with judicial office and erodes public confidence and trust in the Judiciary.”

Based on the “egregious … misconduct in this case, the most appropriate disposition was to remove” Knapp from the bench, Booth wrote.

Knapp’s attorney, William Brennan Jr., declined to comment on the ruling Monday.

Knapp, Gipson and David Duba were all elected in November 2022 to the Anne Arundel County Orphans’ Court, which is made up of three judges who all have an equal voice in decisions reached with the agreement of a majority. Maryland’s orphans’ courts manage estates, wills and sometimes the guardianship of minors after people pass away.

Knapp and Gipson started clashing within a few months, according to the opinion.

By May 2024, Knapp refused to leave the bench between hearings despite Gipson’s request that he do so. The ensuing argument between the two was so loud that people in the Register of Wills office could hear it through the walls.

Gipson called police who, when they arrived, told Knapp to consider his role as a judge and that he’s in the public eye, according to the opinion. Knapp replied that he was “perfectly okay with the public catching onto the crap that goes on in this court,” and added that the “court is non-functioning.”

Gipson was far from the only one to draw Knapp’s ire, according to the opinion. Also in May 2024, Knapp told a former law clerk for the court and Duba, the other sitting judge at the time, that “there’s now a barbed wire fence in between us – you’re on one side, I’m on the other.”

“You’re my enemy now, don’t talk to me,” Knapp said to them, according to the opinion.

The conflict came to a head in June 2024, when Gipson called police to report that Knapp was recording his colleagues without their consent in spite of multiple admonishments. It was then that he deleted recordings in front of the police.

Duba resigned in November 2024 and was replaced by Judge Stacey Scott, appointed in June 2025. Knapp’s removal leaves a vacancy that has yet to be filled.

The Commission on Judicial Disabilities began its investigation into Knapp’s behavior in February 2025 and recommended his removal in March 2025 to the Supreme Court, which did not hold its hearing in the case until June 4, 2026, the same day it ordered him removed.

But Booth wrote Gipson is not “free from blame when it comes to the conflict between them.”

This May, the Commission on Judicial Disabilities recommended that Gipson be removed from the bench, just as it had for Knapp. She has not yet had her hearing before the Maryland Supreme Court, and she did not run for reelection.

Knapp, on the other hand, did – only to finish last out of the four candidates in the Democratic primary for his former seat. That means none of the three elected in 2022 will be on the ballot this November.

“Judges are human and the Maryland Code of Judicial Conduct does not require perfection,” Booth wrote.

“However … when the conduct evidences a pattern or course of conduct that reflects a lack of professionalism, patience, dignity, courteousness and cooperation that is required of a judge, we will not hesitate to find sanctionable conduct,” she wrote.
